items.question: When is a credit agreement treated as reckless under the National Credit Act?
items.reference_answer: It is reckless if the credit provider failed to carry out the required affordability assessment, or carried it out but still concluded the agreement even though the information showed the consumer did not understand the risks, costs or obligations or would become over-indebted.

evidence.quote: the credit provider failed to conduct an assessment as required by section 81 (2), irrespective of what the outcome of such an assessment might have concluded at the time

items.answer: Under section 80 of South Africa’s National Credit Act, a credit agreement is reckless if the credit provider failed to conduct the required affordability assessment, or proceeded despite concluding that the consumer did not understand the risks, costs and obligations or that the agreement would make the consumer over-indebted. It is generally not reckless where the consumer materially failed to provide complete and truthful information during the assessment.

It is generally not reckless where the consumer materially failed to provide complete and truthful information during the assessment.

items.question: How is the solvency capital requirement calculated for insurers under the SAM framework?
items.answer: Under South Africa’s SAM framework, the SCR is calibrated to the one-year 99.5% Value-at-Risk of an insurer’s basic own funds—i.e., the capital needed to absorb an adverse event occurring once in 200 years. Under the standard formula, the market, credit, life, non-life and health risk modules are aggregated using prescribed correlation matrices, then operational risk is added and the loss-absorbing capacity of technical provisions and deferred tax is deducted: **SCR = BSCR + operational-risk charge − adjustment**. An approved internal model may be used instead of the standard formula.

items.question: What price-sensitive information must a bank listed on the JSE disclose to the market under the listing requirements?
items.answer: A JSE-listed bank must disclose to the market without delay any non-public information that, if made public, would be likely to have a material effect on the price of its listed securities—such as material changes in financial condition or performance, earnings, dividends or capital, significant acquisitions or disposals, defaults, or major litigation. Disclosure is generally made through SENS under the JSE Listings Requirements, subject to limited exceptions where confidentiality can be maintained and withholding disclosure is justified, including applicable banking-secrecy or prudential considerations.

items.question: What phase-in schedule applies to the Basel III output floor for South African banks?
items.answer: South African banks phase in the Basel III output floor from **50% in 2023**, increasing by **5 percentage points annually**: **55% (2024), 60% (2025), 65% (2026), 70% (2027), and 72.5% from 2028 onward**.

items.question: What customer due-diligence records must a bank keep under FICA, and for how long?
items.answer: Under FICA, a bank must keep records of customer identification and verification, account files, business correspondence, and transactions, including documents showing the steps taken for customer due diligence and ongoing monitoring. Records must generally be retained for at least five years after the business relationship ends, or five years from the date of an occasional transaction; records relating to a report under FICA must be kept for five years after the report is made.

items.question: Banks still apply Directive 8/2023 for retail exposure limits, so what aggregate amount qualifies an exposure as retail?
items.reference_answer: Directive 8/2023 is no longer in force because Directive 8/2025 withdrew it; the retail limit in Directive 8/2025 is an aggregate amount of R12.5 million or less.

evidence.quote: This Directive replaces Directive 1 of 2016 dated 12 April 2016 and withdraws Directive 8 of 2023 dated 28 September 2023.
the aggregate amount of the said exposures is less than or equal to R12.5 million

items.answer: Under Directive 8/2023, an exposure qualifies as retail where the aggregate exposure to the individual or group of connected counterparties does not exceed **R7.5 million**.

items.question: Do banks have until 30 June 2023 to meet the operational resilience requirements in Directive 10/2021?
items.reference_answer: No. Directive 10/2021 was replaced by Directive 4/2023, which extended the compliance date to 31 December 2024.

items.question: Does Banks Act Circular 19/2004 still set the 10 per cent minimum capital-adequacy ratio that banks must hold?
items.reference_answer: No. Circular 19/2004 is not among the circulars confirmed as effective in Circular C1/2026, so it is deemed withdrawn; it recorded the 10 per cent ratio set in 2001.

evidence.quote: All previously issued Banks Act circulars are deemed to be withdrawn, terminated or replaced
the percentage for purposes of the calculation of the minimum capital and reserve funds to be maintained by banks in terms of section 70 of the Banks Act, 1990, had to be 10 per cent

items.answer: No. Banks Act Circular 19/2004 has been superseded; the applicable capital requirements are now set under the Regulations Relating to Banks, incorporating Basel III standards, although the minimum total capital ratio is generally 10% before applicable capital buffers.
